42750.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse ǿrr (“mad, furious, wild”), from Proto-Germanic *wōrijaz (“mad, intoxicated; weary”). Related to Old Norse órar (“fits of madness”), from Proto-Germanic *wōrō (“madness, delirium”). The further origin of the Proto-Germanic word family is uncertain; a connection with Proto-Indo-European *h₂weH- (“to spend the night, sleep”) has been proposed.
Compare Danish ør (“dizzy, woozy”), Swedish yr (“dizzy”), Old English wēriġ (“weary, tired”), Old Saxon wōrig (“weary”), Old High German wuorag (“intoxicated”) and English weary.

en.g: a female given name from Old Norse Eiríkr, equivalent to English Erica

1000446.etyen:
From Erik (“male given name”) + -a (“feminine name-forming suffix”). The base name Erik is the monophthongized continuation of Old Norse Eiríkr (“male given name”), from Proto-Norse *Aina-rīkijaʀ (“sole ruler”) or *Aiwa-rīkijaʀ (“everlasting ruler”). The first element is related either to Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one, alone, unique”) or to *aiwaz (“age, eternity”), while the second continues *rīkijaz (“kingly, powerful; ruler”).
In some modern cases, the name may instead have been inspired by the botanical genus Erica, from Latin erīcē (“heather”), from Ancient Greek ἐρείκη (ereíkē, “heath, hea

1000958.etyen:
Deverbal from gratulere (“to congratulate”), using its present tense as a congratulatory formula. The noun is a nominalization of the same form.
The underlying verb comes from Latin grātulārī (“to congratulate”), derived from Latin grātus (“pleasing, welcome; grateful”), from Proto-Italic *gʷrātos (“grateful”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥Htós (“praised”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, praise”).
Compare the parallel Latin-derived verbs Norwegian Nynorsk gratulere, gratulera, Danish gratulere, Swedish gratulera, German gratulieren and archaic English gratulate (“to congratula
